titulo: Why do your ears pop on a plane?
receta: mecanismo por dentro con un objeto cotidiano (el oído) y consejo para hoy
destinatario: se lo manda alguien que odia el aterrizaje a su amigo que se duerme en cada descenso, para decirle que por eso le duelen los oídos
fuentes: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia: ear pain from altitude changes
PMC (2019): 'Airplane ear: a neglected yet preventable problem'

frases.texto: Your ears don't pop because of the height. They pop because of trapped air.
Behind each eardrum there's a small pocket of air, linked to the back of your nose by a narrow channel called the eustachian tube.
When the plane climbs, the pressure outside drops, and the extra air behind your eardrum squeezes out through that tube. That's the pop.
On the way down it's the opposite. The tube can get squeezed shut, and that's when your ears feel clogged or hurt.
frases.estilo: Dry, with a hint of sympathy.

frases.texto: The Cleveland Clinic says to swallow, yawn, or chew gum during takeoff and landing, because that helps open the tube.
Heads up: with a cold or a stuffy nose, the tube can swell, so it gets harder to open.
So next flight, start chewing before the descent.
Send this to the friend who sleeps through every landing.
